The midwife bathes and feeds the mother, cleans the room in which she lies with the baby, and sees to it that the necessary piece of iron chain is placed across the doorway of the mother's room. In the mother's bed she places an iron kaśte (sickle) for further protection against malevolent beings or forces. For five days (six, in the case of the Brahmans), the midwife comes to the home in the morning, bathes and feeds the mother, and sees to the baby. At night she returns to her own home to eat and sleep, and other women of the household (or some nearby female relatives) watch over the mother. On the fifth day, known as pāceta, the mother is bathed by the midwife, and all other members of the household also take baths. The napit (barber) comes (to all who live in Ũcu or Brahman pa□ as) and for the first time since the birth, hair, nails, and beards of the members of the household are cut. Ceremonial gifts are given to friends and neighbors, and there is rejoicing in the house. The midwife puts a small amount of dhan (unthreshed rice) by the side of the baby and receives her payment of ten rupees. Once, in the past, she would be paid less for a girl than a boy, but no longer. Brahmans celebrate on the sixth day ( chôtti ) and on the seventh day ( śośthi ) the Brahmans invite kinsmen and make a feast.

p.109.

The family of the Napit (Barber) has been resident in Gôndôgram for four generations. In recent years it has become reduced in number by death and defection, but in the decade preceding the coming of the factory, the Bhandari family of Gôndôgram boasted three adult men able to provide the full services of the Barber jati. They cut hair, beards, and nails, but this was only the beginning of their work. For the household that retains him on a regular basis (the Napit refers to the head of such a household as his jôjman ), he provides many essential services. At all important household ceremonies, from birth through marriage to death, the Napit sees to the grooming of the male members of his jôjman household, and a female member of his family grooms the women. He assists the priests, carrying equipment and assisting in the ceremonies. Finally, he serves the family as a ghô□ ôk (marriage broker), if requested to. His qualifications for this last role derive from the far-flung client network once enjoyed by Gôndôgram's Napits. Prior to 1950, the Gôndôgram Barber family provided its services for the four aforementioned jatis of Gôndôgram and for the bhôdrôlok jatis of five other villages in the area. In one or more of these villages they were certain to have jôjmans of a particular jati represented in Gôndôgram, and so could seek potential spouses. Perhaps more important, as neutrals in the proceedings (not of the families concerned, nor even of the jati) their information was considered better and their judgment more to be trusted.

p.110.

Bauris and Santals visit, at very much irregular intervals, members of their own jatis who have sufficient skill to trim hair. Many men of these jatis trim their own hair and nails. In recent years, those Bauris and Santals with regular employment in or around the factory have taken to patronizing the Bihari barbers who have set up small shops near the factory. More commonly, they patronize the poorest of these, the barbers who conduct their professions by the side of the road, providing customers with a brick or flat stone to sit upon. In Bengali, such a stone or brick is called an i□ , and in schoolboy slang the roadside barber is known as the “Italian barber.”

Fruzzetti, Lina M., and Ákos Östör. 1984. “Kinship and Ritual in Bengal: Anthropological Essays.” 1984, New Delhi. Preprint, South Asian Publishers.

p.189.

Chhatti Din: Muslims in Bengal observe Chhatti, which is more of a celebration. It is the day when the mother will bathe away part of the birth pollution. For the Hindus setera (the sixth) is equivalent to chhatti (which also means the sixth). Though there is no actual worship of Sasthi on this day, the Muslims say that this is Sasthirdin, the day of Sasthi. On this day, mother and child will emerge from the atur ghar to bathe (for the mother this is her first bath since the birth of the child and for the child this is his/her second bath). The dirty clothes which were accumulated in the atur ghar will be washed by the midwife or the dhobi (the Hindu washerman caste). Note here that the Muslims use the Hindu midwife and washermen because of their specific caste occupations. Also on chhatti, the house is cleaned and perhaps whitewashed. The barber woman is called in for kamano (pairing of the mother's and child's nails). At this time, the child's head is shaved and the hair is weighed. In the future, an equal amount of the hair's weight in gold or silver will be given to the poor. This will occur on the child's akika (naming ceremony). The mother has alta (a red dye considered to be auspicious) applied to her feet. Chhatti occurs on the evening of the fifth day after birth. Various members of the Muslim household recite a fatiha known as Sasthir fatiha (a Koranic verse dedicated to Sasthi ). Dirty clothes can be washed and household members are able to touch the mother and the child without fear of pollution, because of the partial purity which takes place on this day. On the other hand, the midwife will not approach the house nor attend to the payoti, (the new mother) again. In the evening a pradip (oil lamp) is lit and kept burning for the duration of that night. On this day the child's future, his/her karma will be written. This is the night when Bidata purus will visit the house where a child is born. How long will the child live? What will be his/her fate and chances in the world, and so forth? The baby's future will be written down including happiness or unhappiness, whether the child will have longevity, and when it will die. A tal pata (pen made from bamboo), ink and a paper or leaf are all placed in a corner of the room next to the lighted lamp. The room has been cleaned for the occasion and members of the family are all in a semi-purified state awaiting the arrival of Bidata Purus. He is the giver of life whereas Sasthi (referred to as his consort) is the protectress of the child's life. The coming of Bidata and the celebration of chhatti parallel each other. “The chhatti or the celebration of the sixth day after the birth of a child, when the mother takes the bath of purification, actually represents deliverance from the dread of a Hindu godling, Chhatti, who personifies the septicaemia which often follows childbirth in unhygenic conditions.” (Ahmad, 1969: 47). A food offering is also left next to the ink and the tal pata for the Bidata. Bidata is an ancestor, a spirit, a higher being with power over a people's life. He is the one who ultimately determines the longevity of the newborn child. In the evening, the maulavi, will recite a fatiha before the arrival of Bidata. It is assumed that he arrives on the night of the fifth day (or on the sixth day) of birth. The next ritual observance is not until the twenty-first day after birth. On that day, the mother and child undergo similar ritual purification. For the Hindu, the twenty-first day bath completes their period of ritual impurities caused by birth, although this is not the case for the Muslims where complete purification is not achieved until the fortieth day. For the duration of forty days, the Muslim mother does not pray namaz nor touch the Koran because of her impure state. On the fortieth day, she will have to observe a few of the Koranic injunctions about her bodily purification, e.g. washing her hair forty times and brushing her teeth with three different sticks forty times. The activities surrounding the bodily purification should be completed before the noon prayers, when the mother will have to pray namaz again. The purification of the mother and the child is now complete, and the mother can again resume her normal work.

p.193.

On the first day of Muharram, Muslims cut their nails (a ritual process) and cleanse themselves. On this day, the men start to work on the tazzia. Tazzia preparations in the town go as far back as thirty or forty years, a time when both Hindus and Muslims jointly prepared them. Today, only the Muslims work on the tazzia but the duldul is still done by the Potidar, who also does the Hindu clay images of the different gods and goddesses. ( Duldul is a clay horse commemorating Imam Hassan's horse, killed at the battle.) The tazzia, is supposed to be the replica of Imam Hassan's tomb, it has the shape of a mausoleum. Depending on the funds available (usually minimal) to spend on the tazzia, it would be decorated with tinsel and glittering paper. Some of these tazzia structures have two or three stories, others as many as ten stories high. The outer frame of the tazzia is made from bamboo sticks. Once the frame is completed, the women begin to decorate it with silver and gold paper. The materials used for decoration now will soon be stored for next year's tazzia. A few years back, the whole tazzia was buried on the last day at Karbala (the desert where Imam Hassan died; in this case the Muslims' burial ground is referred to as Karbala). The actual decorative materials are of no significance to the Muharram festival. One finds the picture of the Taj Mahal or other Mughal buildings stuck on the tazzia, cut out mausoleum shapes of silver or gold tinsel are attached. A curtain is put up to the entrance of the tazzia though the inside is hollow and contains no objects. One of the paras has a cloth tazzia. The frame of this tazzia is that of the Bangla (hut or house, shaped after the local Bengali style houses), and the frame is covered with a red cloth. This type tazzia is a new idea recently introduced to the town.

p.232.

Chhatti Din. Muslims in Bengal observe chhatti, a celebration. It is the day when the mother bathes away a part of the birth pollution. For the Hindus setera (the sixth) is equivalent to chhatti (which also means the sixth). Though there is no actual worship of Sasthi on this day, the Muslims say that this is Sasthir din, the day of Sasthi. On this day, mother and child will emerge from the atur ghar to bathe, for the mother this is her first bath since the birth of the child and for the child this is his/her second bath. The dirty clothes which were accumulated in the atur ghar will be washed by the midwife or the dhoba (Hindu washerman caste). Also on chhatti, the house is cleaned and perhaps whitewashed. The barber woman is called in for Kamano (pairing of the mother's and child's nails). At this time, the child's head is shaved and the hair is weighed. In the future, an equal amount of the hair's weight in gold or silver will be given to the poor. This will occur on the child's akika (naming ceremony). The mother has alta (a red dye considered to be auspicious) applied to her feet. Chhatti occurs on the evening of the fifth day of the birth. Various members of the Muslim household recite a fatiha known as Sasthir fat ha (a Koranic verse for Sasthi). Dirty clothes can be washed on this day. Household members are able to touch the mother and child without fear of pollution, because of the partial purity which takes place on this day. Furthermore, the midwife will not approach the house nor attend to the payoti (the new mother) again. In the evening a pradip (an oil lamp) is lit and kept burning for the duration of that night. On this day the child's future, his/her karma, will be written. This is the night when Bidata purus will visit the house where a child is born. How long will the child live? What are his/her fate, chances in the world and so forth? His entire future will be written down including happiness or unhappiness, whether the child will have longevity, and when or what it will die of. A tal pata (pen made from bamboo), ink and a paper or leaf are all laid down in a corner of the room next to the lighted lamp. The room has been cleaned for the occasion and the members are all in a semi-purified state awaiting the arrival of Bidata Purus. He is the giver of life whereas Sasthi (referred to as his consort) is the protecteress of children's life. The coming of Bidata and the celebration of chhatti parallel each other. “The celebration of the sixth day after the birth of a child, when the mother takes the bath of purification, actually represents deliverance from the dread of a Hindu godling, Chhatti, who personifies the septicaemia which often follows childbirth in unhygenic conditions.” (Ahmad, 1969: 47). Food offering is left next to the ink and the tal pata for the Bidata. Bidata is an ancestor, a spirit, a higher being with power over people's life. He has an ultimate say in the longevity of a newborn child. In the evening, the maulavi will recite a fatiha before the arrival of Bidata. It is assumed that he arrives on the night of the fifth or sixth day of birth. The next ritual observance is not until the twenty-first day after birth. On that day, mother and child undergo similar ritual purifications. For the Hindu, the bath on the twenty-first day completes the time of ritual impurity caused by birth, although this is not the case for the Muslims where complete purification is achieved only on the fortieth day. For forty days, the Muslim mother does not pray namaz nor touch the Koran because of her impure state. On the fortieth day, she will have to observe a few of the Koranic injunctions about bodily purification, washing herself from head to toe forty times, cutting her nails forty times, washing her hair forty times and brushing her teeth with three different sticks forty times. The activities surrounding bodily purification should be completed before the noon prayers, when the mother will have to pray namaz again. The purification of the mother and the child is now complete, and the mother can again resume her normal work.

p.236.

The midwife can use the skull of a cow to represent Jebra, the counterpart of Sasthi. On the twenty-first day, the midwife immerses the deity in the nearby pond. Jebra stands for the negative aspect whereas Sasthi is the positive aspect of the deity. Jebra's wrath can kill both the mother and child, but Sasthi's might protects them. Women claim that the deity is so powerful that one must worship the negative side of Sasthi before paying homage to the other aspect. Some Hindu gods come in pairs, where one is benign and the other is malevolent. 8 8. The diverse kinds and categories of relatives in Bengal are further elaborated on in Fruzzetti, Ostor, Barnett, 1976. Varying relatives are affected by pollution in different degrees. On the fifth day (the evening, which becomes the sixth day after birth) the priest enters the cleansed and purified atur ghar (purified with water and cow dung) to perform the ritual of Setera, (Sasthi). First, the Brahman priest makes an image of the deity with cow dung and cowrie shells on the inside wall of the atur ghar, five or twenty-one couries being used to complete the image. Mother and child bathe and wear clean clothes. The barber woman is called to the house for kamano, pairing nails and applying red dye to the mother's feet. Next, the mother and child attend the ritual performed by the priest, after which they are partially purified. From that day on, they can sit in the sun even though they are still in a polluted state. The clothing used or worn during the five polluted days will be washed by the washerman. This completes the semi-purification. From the fifth day on, the rest of the jnati, (male linked relatives) are purified. On the evening of the fifth day (the sixth day) Muslims and Hindus await the coming of Bidata purus who will write the child's fate ( karma ). Hindus consider Bidata a sacred person, a god. He is paired with Sutika Sasthi (the Sasthi of birth) as husband and wife (similar to the Muslims' view). The deities protect the mother and child, but the Hindus take additional items as a precaution against other spirits who can inflict harm. These items are the iron bangle, the colirium holder, the fishermen's net and the amulets, all of which one also finds used by the Muslims.

### Gond

Elwin, V. (1947). The Muria and their ghotul. Oxford University Press.

p.376.

In Pupgaon, the combing was much gentler, and was only done every three days. In Bandopal, the girls did not tap the head but twisted the comb through the hair and rubbed the scalp in a very soothing way. When we were at Binjhli they were not combing at all, and in Khutgaon after a dog had relieved itself on the leader's turban, the Siraha forbade the girls to touch the chelik's heads. But generally the combing is done in the way I have described. When a lot of girls are at it together, the clicking of the combs against a score of hard heads makes a remarkable noise, reminding me of a phrase by Roy Campbell: While her sharp nails, in slow caresses ruled, Prowl through his hair with sharp electric clicks.

p.390.

The next morning the Kotwar went to a wild fig tree to extract its sticky, milky gum. He struck a branch with the blunt end of his axe and caught some drops of gum in a leaf-cup. He brought this back and sat down by a fire. He spread the gum on either side of the comb with a bit of straw, warmed it on the fire, applied more gum, laid the silver paper over it and rubbed it in hard with the handle of his chisel till the pattern showed. He repeated the process on the opposite side toasting the comb before the fire by sticking it on the end of his chisel. Finally he brought out the pattern clearly by pressing in the silver paper with his own finger-nails, and washed it with a straw dipped in water.

Fuchs, Stephen. 1960. The Gond and Bhumia of Eastern Mandla. 1960, Bombay, New York. Asia Pub. House. 

p.218.

Meanwhile, the other people who have now assembled at the house take the outcaste to a near river or pond ( nala ). All the way the villagers and nat relatives abuse him and throw pieces of cow-dung and mud at him. They chase him up-river and back again. Then they make the outcaste sit on a boulder or stone in the middle of the river. There the master of ceremonies himself cuts with a knife or razor the hair of the culprit at four spots on the forehead, at the neck, and at the temples. If the outcaste does not want to have his head shaved entirely—a ceremony regarded as particularly degrading—he has to pay one and a quarter rupee to the sonwani. But if the offence of the outcaste has been very serious, his whole body must be shaved, even his scalplock and the hair under his armpits. A woman also is shaved in the same manner by the sonwani. After that he pares the outcaste's toe- and finger-nails.

p.249.

The Gond and Panka, not however the Bhumia, call the barber ( nau ) on the thirteenth day after the birth. He cuts the hair of the child, and also of the child's father and other male relatives, and pares the finger- and toe-nails of its mother. If the barber is not available, the nat relatives do it instead. A washerman ( dhobi ) is called to wash the clothes of all in the house. If the washerman cannot come, they take him a cloth which he must wash. The other clothes may then be washed at home. A Brahmin is invited to recite some prayers (‘to read something out of a book’, my Gond informants said). It is for the child's health. The villagers are invited for a meal, or get at least some liquor or sugar. 1 1 This is a custom common to all non-tribal castes in Mandla District. Cf. Russell and Hiralal (1916): Vol. 4, p. 136.

p.336.

Then the nat relatives of the deceased go to the cremation ground. They collect the bones which were not consumed by the fire, usually the skull and the spine, and with the ashes form a pile which they cover with stones. Then all the guests proceed to the bathing place of the village. There the master of ceremonies shaves the hair of the head (except the skull lock), beard, and hair on the body of all the deceased's kinsmen. He pares their finger- and toe-nails. No one may be omitted, even if the number of kinsmen is large. After that the master of ceremonies bathes them. This ceremony much resembles the purification of an outcaste. And indeed, before this purificatory bath is given, no one of the deceased's kinsmen may remove grain from the bins or sow his field.

### Kerala

Parpola, Marjatta. 2000. “Kerala Brahmins in Transition: A Study of a Namputiri Family.” In Studia Orientalia. 2000, Helsinki. Finnish Oriental Society.

p.267.

A new clean dress is, of course, a very common symbol of a new status, and it is a constant symbol in Indian domestic rituals. The universal symbolism of bathing and cutting the hair and nails in rites of passage is that of separation from the previous role by removing surface dirt, purification. Manu (4,221) has a comparison: The food of those other persons who have been successively enumerated as such whose food must not be eaten, the wise declare (to be as impure as) skin, bones, and hair. (Transl. Bühler 1886: 163–164.)

p.279.

The Kerala customs according to Gundert include the following information. Kerala Brahmins have no moustache, but they can let their hair grow behind or their nails grow long if they wish (10). The Veda-less Brahmins, the so called pa﻿ṭ﻿ṭan Brahmins, who are lower than the Nampūtiris, wear their hairlock at the back of their hair, while the Nampūtiris wear a forelock (18). Kerala Brahmins could be half-shaven, i.e. have only their head and chest shaven contrary to the custom of the Brahmins in other regions of India (56), and a Brahmin could get himself shaven after noon was passed (52).

...

When a Nampūtiri woman was pregnant, the husband and another Nampūtiri used to say prayers and perform rituals every day for the sake of good progeny. The prospective father used to let his beard, hair and nails grow. This is called garbha-dīkṣa. There were many other situations where a male person was supposed to remain unshaven in India, like the brahmacarya period and the dīkṣa. I understood from what NNA said that cutting of these bodily margins, dangerous as such, was counted as an act of violence as well, as was speaking harshly and cutting trees. (NNA, p. 26.)

p.292.

NNA's dress, when he became a kind of hermit, did not change compared to the dress that he was wearing in his previous life stage, as he continued to live in his own house, and did not move to live in the forest. As will be remembered, Manu prescribed a skin or a tattered garment and the hair to be in braids, and the body-hair, beard, and nails to be unclipped. 

p.300.

Fawcett (1900: 41–42) mentions a ring hanging on a string in front of the throat of a boy of 12. This ornament, he says, was put on in the sixth month when the boy was named, and would be worn until he was 15. As baby boys and girls were dressed in the same way, it was difficult to tell their gender. For this reason baby boys wore a distinctive golden neck ornament. This ornament is called puliyā mōtiraṃ ‘tiger ring’ and it is made of gold. The boy started to wear the ring in the annaprāśana ceremony, and wore it until the samāvartana. They have become rare but can still be seen. Puliyā mōtiraṃ was only worn on special occasions, like birthdays, in addition to the simple ring which was worn all the time. Tiger nails may have been used in this ornament, but they have been substituted with imitations. Mention was earlier made of a pendant of palāśa wood given to the boy in his samāvartana ceremony.

### Kol

Griffiths, Walter G., and B. S. (Biraja Sankar) Guha. 1946. “The Kol Tribe of Central India.” In Monograph Series, vol. 2. 1946, Calcutta. Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal.

p.61.

The Sixth Day Ceremony: Chhatthi. After six days it is believed that the greatest period of danger is over and the woman can begin to make preparations to take up her normal life. This period corresponds with the time of greatest physical danger, for by the sixth day after birth, the dreaded septicaemia, if it is to come, will make its appearance. When day has come and all is well the dhobi and the nai are usually sent for. The former takes all the soiled clothes. The wife, after a preliminary bath and anointing by the dai, puts on fresh clothes. The barber trims the nails of her hands and feet and puts vermilion on both her feet and the feet of her child so that no evil spirit may harm them as they make their way to the place of the ceremonial bath. Her head has been oiled with til oil and occasionally the child has been pricked on the stomach with a hot iron, so that “the waters may be digested”. All the earthen vessels in the house should be thrown out and new ones purchased from the Kumhar, and the house should be cleaned and plastered. The nai also gives the male members of the family a good shave, both of the face and the head.

p.123.

FUNERAL FEAST ( Din Pani ). If the deceased was a male the funeral feast occurs on the tenth day after the death, and if a female on the ninth day. The time of the feast after a child's death is not so uniform. Unless the child is grown up and rather important, it is not usual to have a feast; or if there is one it is a private one within the home. But in the case of adults such a feast must always be given, otherwise the honour of the tribe would be tainted, and the family rebuked by the panch. On the morning of the feast preparations for it are made in the house. The home is plastered, the barber is called and the faces are shaved and the nails of both hands and feet are pared. A special bath is taken and clean clothes put on. The people who are invited to such a feast are usually only relatives, though occasionally a larger group of the deceased's tribal friends may be invited. Others, who do not actually eat, are there to watch and talk, making quite a crowd. Special food has been prepared, and the things tabooed during the period of mourning are freely made use of and eaten at the feast. Hereafter all the members of the household, except the chief mourner, may freely partake of any food and there are no restrictions. The chief mourner eats this food at the feast, but for a year following must continue to observe the food taboos of the first ten days as noted above. There are no dishes or food peculiar to the funeral feast; it and the wedding feast may be much alike as far as the kinds of foods are concerned—rice, pulse, curries, of either vegetables or meats, puris, bara, dahi, chapatis, and the like. The presence of a large group is considered desirable and is a sign of solidarity.

### Tamil

Jacob-Pandian, Ebenezer Titus. 1972. Dravidianization: A Tamil Revitalization Movement. 1972, Ann Arbor, Mich. University Microfilms International. p.146.

The Labbay Muslims gave great importance to reading scripture and to having special prayers. They also gave special significance to the process of eating together from a common pot ( sahan ). The Labbay placed great value on their women having black teeth, which they acquired by rubbing on them a black powder called tasanaa. Marutani, a red substance taken from leaves, was applied to beautify the nails and palms, a practice performed by Hindus and Christians as well.

Gough, Kathleen. 1969. “Caste in a Tanjore Village.” 1969, Cambridge, England. Preprint, Published for the Department of Archaeology and Anthropology at the University Press. p.23.

Barbers were required to shave the body hair and a portion of the head hair and to manicure the finger-nails of Brahman and non-Brahman men, twice a month, and to shave the heads of Brahman widows at similar intervals. They were also herbalists, leeches and dentists. Women of the caste were midwives for all castes above Ādi Drāvidas. Carpenters made wooden ploughs, bullock-carts, paddy-storage chests and other wooden utensils, and doors, window-frames and pillars for houses. Though they did odd jobs for all the castes, their work was overwhelmingly for Brahmans. For in this period few families other than Brahmans owned ploughs or bullock-carts, and only Brahman houses had doors and window-frames. Even today, most non-Brahman and Pallan families live in windowless, thatched mud shacks and hang a grass mat before the doorway.

Dhanasekaran, S. 1965. “Visavanoor.” In Census of India 1961, No. 14, Vol. 9. no. 14. 1965, Delhi. Manager of Publications. p.32.

60. Tatooing was once commonly practised on women and children of both sexes; grown up men rarely have their hands tatooed. However, this has gone out of fashion; women of Pallans, Parayans and Chakkiliyans, are more fond of tattooing; they have their arms elaborately tatooed with ornamental designs of beautiful flowers and figures. Men tatoo the inner side of their arms with their names inscribed; among Christians, Parayas have a fascination towards tatooing and the device is very often a cross ! With children, it is confined to a simple line drawn down from the forehead. Tatooing is not common among Protestant Christians. Most of the men, now-a-days, have their hair cropped and only a few Chettiars and Brahmins have Kudumi or tuft on the head. Muslims have completely shaven heads with beard, while the Hindus wear only the moustache on the face but seldom or never wear a beard. Among Hindus, wearing of a beard very often indicates some vows. Men wear Kadukkans or ear-rings made of gold with some beads or pearls, but this is the fashion among the wealthier section of the community. Thayathu or the charm is also worn by many; of course, some religious sentiments are attached to it. Use of cosmetics and toilet is quite restricted to girls of younger generation, some educated women and teachers and a vast majority of women folk are not at all aware of modern cosmetics. Most of the_Hindu women, after their bath, smear their faces and feet with a solution of turmeric, which is supposed to make them fair. Toilet soap is not used nor they apply snow or Talcum powder after their bath. The finger nails are reddened with a dye of Maruthani leaves, a kind of tree. Women usually have the feet uncovered. They, of course, pay sufficient attention to hair-dressing, but, of course, women of low castes do not do hair-dressing frequently. Women generally tie up their long black glossy hair in a knot at the back of the head, which is called Kondai. This is not, however, in vogue among young girls and school going children; they generally plait their hair in tails or Jadai hanging down behind, scarcely with any ribbons at the end. Only a handful of girls of wealthy families use ribbons and jadai-billais; beautiful flowers of sweet fragrance are tastefully placed in the hair which have a very pleasing effect, but as flowers have to come from distant places and the village has got no flower gardens, not all wear flowers and only a few can afford to buy flowers for cash; on festival days and important occasions, flowers are common.

### Telugu

Tapper, Bruce Elliot. 1987. “Rivalry and Tribute: Society and Ritual in a Telegu Village in South India.” In Studies in Sociology and Social Anthropology. 1987, Delhi. Hindustan Pub.Corp. 

p.127.

Members of the Barber caste from Yatapalem begin drumming as the groom's family barber scrapes each nail on the groom's toes and fingers. A close male relative of the groom, such as his elder brother, then puts a wad of paper money into the sari end of the groom's kinsman called atta , a classificatory mother-in-law (or mother of a marriageable relative) such as the groom's father's sister. The barber then snips the hair at the sides of the groom's head, in a perfunctory manner since he does not actually need a haircut. The drumming then stops. At this point the groom is jokingly smeared with some pot soot by his sister or other close relative to make him imperfect and less vulnerable to evil eye. The barber then smears the groom with nalugu , a paste used in bathing that contains turmeric, sesame oil, and crushed black gram ( minapa pindi or Phaseolus mungo). The auspicious woman helps to smear turmeric on the bride and then is smeared with turmeric herself by a relative of the bride such as an elder sister. At this point, the barber is given a payment of the rice from the wooden measuring container which he wraps in a white cloth.

p.135.

On the third day of the wedding, the first ceremony is for the removal of the kanka n am wrist threads and bāsikālu forehead pads. Between 10 and 11 a.m. the groom and bride sit on a cloth which covers the seating platforms on the pen d l i pīnu. They are separated by an auspicious wife who sits in the middle on the overturned grindstone. In a repetition of the nail-cutting ceremony, the groom, auspicious wife, and bride are smeared with turmeric and nalugu. After the groom is playfully smeared with pot soot by his wife's elder brother, with whom he has a joking relationship, a canopied procession goes to a well to fetch water in three pots. Madiga, Barber and Jangam drummers lead the procession of the two ceramic and one brass pot each with a turmeric root tied to its rim just as in the nail-cutting ceremony. The pots are placed down on small piles of unhusked rice, turmeric is added to their water which is mixed between them, and a thread is tied connecting them. The groom's Barber washes him with water from the pots. Then the bride is bathed by female relatives of the groom. At this point several babies are also washed in the highly auspicious water. As water is poured into their hands in addition to yellow rice, the groom and then the bride are made to face each of the four cardinal directions to perform dan d am salutes to deities in each. Deities mentioned are dēvu d u , (‘god’, meaning Rama), and the village goddesses—Bandamma, Ravalamma, Maridamma, and Bangaramma.

p.144.

The passing of auspicious influences by touch is discernible in the touching of the groom and bride with rice pounding poles by auspicious wives when they sing the suvvi song during the nail-cutting ceremony. Auspicious wives are also encouraged to touch the bride's wedding locket before it is tied around her neck.

Hiebert, Paul G. 1971. Konduru: Structure and Integration in a South Indian Village. 1971, Minneapolis. University of Minnesota Press.

p.85.

The Barber is the village gossip. He calls at the clean-caste homes with his little metal box of knives, brushes, soap, and mirrors. There he shaves the farmer, cuts his hair, trims finger and toe nails, pulls teeth, lances boils, and performs other minor surgery. He must take care to dispose of the clippings properly lest the jajman's enemies use these in destructive magic against their owner. Not quite in jest the people say, “There was a burglary at the Barber's house last night; three pots of combings were stolen!” Barbers do not go to Harijan homes; however, the Harijans use the Barbers’ tools in return for a small share of the harvest.

p.87.

The Barber measures out a gift share, four to six fans of grain, for shaving the household males and a poli cherta for ritual performances. He pulls aside his bonus (addam dωsili) “for showing the mirror” to his prosperous masters so they can have the privilege of observing their tonsure while it is taking place. Since the poor do not give a bonus at harvesttime, they are shaved without the benefits of soap or a mirror. The Barber does more than shaving, however; his knife is used at births to sever the umbilical cord while his wife assists in the delivery of the child. After funerals he shaves his clients at the time of their purification. But it is at weddings that he is most needed. He prepares the groom and is given small gifts of grain, liquor, coins, and the clothes that the young man had been wearing. He pares the nails of the couple during the ceremonies and claims the unhusked rice used in making the ritual designs. He arranges for a Barber band to play for the ceremony and also for the many processions that welcome the bridal party, that fetch the ceremonial pots and sacred earth, that accompany the wedding party to the temple, and that parade the newlyweds through town. Finally, on an auspicious day fixed by the family purohit , the Barber performs the ritual tonsure and receives the groom's turban as a symbol of his assumption of the jajmani rights over the new home.

### Toda

Rivers, W. H. R. (William Halse Rivers). 1906. The Todas. 1906, London; New York. Macmillan. 

p.268.

In one of the methods of sorcery which have been described it will be remembered that human hair is used. The Todas take the same kind of precautions about hair and nail-parings which are so widely spread throughout the world, but the reasons for the precautions differed from those usually given. I was told that the Todas do not ordinarily cut their hair, but the heads of children are shaved and adults also shave their heads on special occasions. The hair removed at these times is hidden in bushes or hollows in the rocks, and the reason given is that it may not be taken by crows.

p.269.

Nail-parings are buried in the ground, and this is done in order that they may not be eaten by the buffaloes, for “nails are poisonous to buffaloes,” who will die or become ill if they find them when grazing.

Marshall, William E. (William Elliot). 1873. A Phrenologist amongst the Todas. 1873, London. Longmans, Green. p.50.

A pretty sight, that rewarded one of my expeditions, was a group of women and girls just returned from the stream, sitting, clean and bright, curling one another's hair. The locks were separated neatly, and the partings made accurately with the finger-nail. Each lock having been dressed straight, either with the fingers or a forked stick, is twisted and twisted until it has formed a tight coil, when the end is tucked in among the roots. The well developed female back-head looks remarkably pleasing under this treatment—unadorned, adorned the most. The curls are opened out in the morning.

### Uttar Pradesh

Opler, Morris Edward, and Rudra Datt Singh. 1952. “Economic, Political and Social Change in a Village of North Central India.” Human Organization: Journal of the Society for Applied Anthropology Vol. 11 (2): 2. p.9.

Old, traditional forms of ornament are going out of fashion as modern styles of necklaces and earrings become popular. There is a great shift by those who can afford them towards the use of gold rather than silver ornaments. Women use plastic pins in the hair and nail lacquer. Some of the young women even use lipstick. There is also a change in women's hair style. The bun at the back of the head has gone out of fashion and instead the hair is done in braids which hang loose, frequently tied with ribbons.


## Southeast Asia

### Balinese

Covarrubias, Miguel. 1938. Island of Bali. 1938, New York. Alfred A. Knopf. p.119.

When a Balinese has nothing to do he squats on the ground and pulls hairs from his face with two coins or with special tweezers, and women remove the hair under the armpits with porous volcanic stones. Some men wear moustaches, which are considered elegant, but only priests wear beards. It is a sign of distinction to wear the fingernails long, often four inches or more, showing that the wearer does not have to do manual work. Priests may wear the nails of both hands long, but the average well-to-do Balinese lets them grow only on the left hand. In Tenganan I have seen young girls wearing nail-protectors five inches long made of solid gold.

One also should not cut his nails at night for fear of them dying soon. In Pebato people said about this that then the totokesi , an ominous night-bird, would take the nails cut off “in order to use them itself for nails” 4 . That the Toradja still feel that hair is a source of strength is apparent from a custom that has come into existence only since the arrival of the Government. If a Toradja fears that a horse other than his own will win a prize, he tries to get possession of a hair from the mane or the tail of that animal, and he ties this to the mane or the tail of his own horse. Through this, not the other one, but his own animal will win.

p.362.

A good day is chosen for the wedding. People sometimes go to consult the Boeginese /Buginese/ kotika for this, but usually the wedding is set for the new or full moon, or one of the days of the waxing moon. On the day of the wedding the bridegroom is led to the house of the bride by kin group and friends. It has been determined ahead of time whether this escort will take place in the morning or in the evening; usually it is done in the evening. The female members of the kin group and friends go unimpeded to the stairs of the dwelling of the bride, where they /249/ are strewn with rice; the bridegroom himself and his male companions are stopped on the way by young boys and slaves, who, with spears and sticks held across the path, prevent the procession from continuing. By offering cotton, plates, and duits the boys are induced to take away the obstacles. Because the ransom is set high, there must be much bargaining, and this is accompanied by much noise. The stopping is called mejawa , and the gift that is given for being let through is called pelawa . The procession is also stopped on the stairs of the dwelling; here a larger gift must be given for being allowed through. When the bridegroom and his people arrive, the nails of the guests are colored red ( mokolontigi ) 40 . Kolontigi is not Boeginese /Buginese/. The plant from whose leaves the red dyestuff is obtained is called in that language pátji (Mal. patjar , “henna”). Kolontigi is a corruption of the Makassarese karoentigi , Lawsonia Alba, nat. fam. of the Lythraceae. . Sometimes this is done as early as the day preceding that of the wedding.

p.374.

The corpse is placed on a few pieces of bamboo; there it is washed and wrapped in white cotton. The corpse of a man is laid out by men, that of a woman by women. The wash-water has mixed in it things that are used in doing one’s toilet, such as rice flour, called bada (Mal. bedak ), alindaki , or posani , a tree whose bast foams in water and which is therefore used in the manner of soap; lemo ntjoesoe , a kind of lemon, with whose juice people clean the hair; kolontigi , with which the nails are colored red, and damedaloe , a kind of wood that is also used for cleansing the body. The 257 corpse is wet with this water three times while a do’a is said, and is then washed. After that it is wrapped in a cloth according to certain rules: first the head is wrapped, then the body, finally the feet. Then this shroud is tied first around the neck, then around the middle together with the wrists, then around the knees, and finally around the feet. Then the ones who have done this work go to bathe.

p.601.

Some people keep their child’s hair and nails in a little basket ( dompipi ) or in their clothing basket ( roko ). In Onda’e there are families where the first hair of all the children is kept as a sort of genealogical register, so as to know how many members the stock has numbered; thus, for the same reason, the hair of the deceased may be kept 419 (XVI, 16). We were told that when the kin group has accumulated a hundred packets of such hair, a meal is held “in order to remember the mercifulness of the Lord (Poee).” There are also mothers who plait the hair into a string ( oloewoe ) and were this around their necks.

p.602.

When hair and nails of the baby are cut for the first time, a good day must be chosen for this. It must not in any case take place on Kakoenia (14th day); also not when the field is planted or at the time of the harvest. Before one starts cutting, the child’s crown and forehead are spit upon ( rasoepa ) with finely chewed wild cinnamon ( pakanangi ); the little nails are pressed into a piece of curcuma or ginger, or they are rubbed with it. Then with a sliver of bamboo ( djimoejoe ) one cuts off some hair and scrapes the nails with it; after that the work may be continued with an iron knife, after this has been counted off from 1 -- 7. If iron were used immediately, the child would become a crosspatch ( taoe masii ). Nowadays scissors are used for this. One must let the hair on the crown stand, “so that the tanoana will have a support ( pangkekeninja ).” If father or mother do not cut the hair and nails of their child themselves, the one who does it must receive a reward, “so that the child’s tanoana will be cool.” Sometimes this reward is a resin torch, “so that the person will not become blind.” Some children, it is said, become thin after the cutting of their hair and nails. This comes about because their tanoana has gone away with the hair; it must then be enticed back with rice and egg 7 . Children also become thin if father and mother are repeatedly unkind ( masii ) to them. If, for example, a father becomes angry at his child because it does not immediately do what it has been instructed to do and he even threatens to kill it, then the child becomes thin and weak and the skin gets a yellow color.

This passage introduces us to jewellery, which forms a part ethnologically very important in Malay dress, and which may be studied preeminently in the dress of bride and bridegroom. Again the Perak court has preserved tradition. Both sexes wear the dragon-headed armlet 1 1 Pontoh b˘ernaga and pontoh. as it occurs in Java; both sexes wear a long gold chain of Javanese name 2 2 K˘engkalong. tucked into the waist-band on the left side. Besides these, they wear a number of other ornaments which differ not in character but only in quality from those used by lesser folk. Both sexes, as in Java, wear an oval buckle, 1 1 P˘ending. or rather ornament of gold or silver or jadam -ware or even brass, according to their rank and means: the older specimens all having conventionalised lotus-flower centres, others the signs of the Zodiac, and some of jadam an Arabic text. Both sexes wear hollow anklets 2 2 K˘eronchong. and bracelets 3 3 G˘elang kana b˘ertunjal b˘erk˘erawang b˘erpahat t˘erus b˘ersiku k˘eluang dua tingkat. such as occur in Java; but the bride wears, in addition, peculiar bracelets, 4 4 G˘elang b˘ersudu. a badge of virginity, whose ends are shaped like the side of a flat triangular spoon. Both sexes wear a breast ornament 5 5 Dokoh. worn in Java, consisting of tiers of gold plates, and above it, as in Java, an ornament 6 6 Agok. commonly worn by children, circular 7 7 Bunga kiambang. for male, crescent-shaped for female, of gold filigree-work. In place of turban, the bride wears a gold (or gilt-paper) frontlet 8 8 K˘elat dahi ( gandek, Mal.) upon her brows, like that used both by bride and groom in Java; it is surmounted by a garden of paper blossoms 9 9 Bunga k˘etar. stuck on nodding wires; and gold flowers are fixed by golden hair-pins 10 10 Pachak tunggal; tumang s˘endok. on the top of her chignon. Both sexes wear a variety of rings, some plain and dubbed after their shapes, the “sated leech” 11 11 Chinchin pachat k˘enyang. (on the index finger of the right hand), the “elephant-foot bezel” 12 12 Ch. tapak gajah. (on the little finger of the same hand); some set with stones and called, for example, “the garden of fire-flies” 13 13 Kunangkunang sa-kabun. on the ring-finger. The bride also wears a ring remarkable for a ruby-eyed filigree gold peacock 14 14 M˘erak. perched in place of a bezel; a ring which is always worn along with a protector 15 15 Changgal (vide “Malay Magic,” p. 46). for the long finger-nail of leisure that looks like a glorified cheese-scoop. “They wore a girdle of gold and golden rings in their ears,” we are told of the kings and nobles of Langgasu. At the foundation of Palembang both sexes were adorned with ear-rings but now the bride only wears ear-rings, 1 1 Subang. round, the size of a penny, a badge of virginity, and these are giving way to small drops 2 2 Subang gantong. and pendants. 3 3 Orlit. The bridegroom's dagger 4 4 In Patani he wears the Tajong or ‘kingfisher’ hilted k˘eris. may have a golden sheath and gold or ivory haft: for is he not a king for the day?

p.49.

Such is the older jewellery. Perak tradition vaguely ascribes most of it to craftsmen immigrant from Java, and old Malacca of course not only represented the Palembang tradition, with its Indo-Javanese culture, but also had a Javanese settlement. Clearly gold work exhibits styles quite different from that of the foliated scrolls common to Malay silver, and, curiously enough, Indian influence is patent in the Sanskrit names for gold pinchbeck and jewels but not in the terminology of silver. But if most of the wedding finery be derived from Java, there must be other old elements on which comparative investigation should throw further light. Whence comes the virgin's bracelet with flat triangular spoonlike ends? Whence the cheese-scoop nail protector and the peacock ring?

p.76.

As for the dress of the bride—First of all, an old wise-woman sets to work to dispel all evil influences: Portuguese thread of several colours is tied at the bride's neck; two candles are stuck before a looking-glass; sacrificial water is sprinkled; saffron rice strewn; the old woman takes and waxes seven long hairs and then clips them off. (Now if the end of the hairs fall towards the bride or the stump of hair remaining move after the clipping, it is a sign the girl has been deflowered, but if the clipped tresses fell straight outwards and the stumps do not move, then she is a maiden.) After that, her front-hair and her eye-brows are dressed and the short curling hair at the back of her neck is arranged in the shape of a sparrow's tail. Her hair is done into a roll. She is invested in bride's dress: silk trousers of Achinese cut, gold threaded at the bottom, and with the ‘duck-web’; a gold threaded silk skirt of fine, small pattern; a crimson jacket stamped with gold-leaf with quilted collar, the edge of collar and wrists adorned with jewelled gold work; a scarf of cloth-of-gold or of the lime pattern interwoven with gold and with heavy gold-threaded border; a crescent-shaped pendant ornament; twelve tiers of gold breast-plates; a bead necklace of gold; nine rows of gold bean necklace; a long chain tucked into the waist-band; a Manilla chain of five rows; three rows of a necklace of gold coin-like discs; fine Arabian belt; on each arm four rows of solid gemmed gold bracelets with spoon-like ends; on each upper arm a gold armlet with snake's-head ends; hollow gold anklets; a large, round gemmed gold earring; on the index-finger of the right hand a plain, thick, round gold ring; on the little finger of the right hand a ring set with rubies and other precious stones; on the little finger-nail of the left hand a nail-guard surmounted by a jewelled filigree peacock; rings set with small rubies on every finger; on her brow a gold gem-studded frontlet; and above her chignon gold jewelled flowers. When all is ready, the bride is seated on a golden mat and fanned by her maidens so that she may not swelter under her excess of clothing.

Wilkinson, R. J. (Richard James). 1920. “Life and Customs: The Incidents of Malay Life.” In Papers on Malay Subjects. 1920, Singapore. Kelly and Walsh. p.29.

The morning of the fourth day is taken up with the ceremonial shaving 1 1 Andam. of the bride's fringe and with her adornment for the festivities of the evening. Her hair to the width of a finger's breadth all round the forehead is drawn forward and shaved off, while the band plays special tunes in honour of the event. After this shaving is over, the bride puts on her bridal dress and jewellery. She wears a goldembroidered jacket with tight sleeves, a pair of loose silk trousers and a silk sarong. In her hair she fixes a number of artificial flowers of tinsel-work, kept in position by wires; to her ears she attaches the heavy, round ear-studs 2 2 Subang. that are the emblems of virginity. On her arms, over her tight sleeves, she puts an assortment of bracelets and anklets, notably, if she is a Perak raja, dragon-shaped armlets ( pontoh ). She is adorned with golden nail-protectors, with hollow anklets, with necklaces, with three breast ornaments known as dokoh, and with as much additional jewellery as her mother can borrow. 3 3 Nowadays there is great variety in bridal costume, even in Perak, to which these words apply.

Winstedt, Richard. 1961. The Malay Magician: Being Shaman, Saiva and Sufi. 1961, London. Routledge and Kegan Paul. p.16.

Oddly enough while it is tabu ( pantang ) to allude to the beauty or health of an infant for fear of inviting the malice of some jealous spirit, there is no ban on mentioning his vitality. ‘My goodness, what vitality he has!’— Wah! semangat —is a common term of admiration for children. The absence of any ban on its use would appear to be part and parcel of an almost scientific attitude towards vital force considered as impersonal and devoid of individual will, soul or spirit. For the primitive Malay looking below the outer aspect of man and beast and plant and stone found in all of them an energizing power that permeated them like electricity. It is possessed by all things ‘in widest commonalty spread’. There is no ‘rank, condition or degree’ to distinguish the vital force in man from the vital force in rice or the vital force in an animal. Nor is the idea of immortality associated with it. But certain objects like stones and tough plants and certain parts of the body like the teeth and hair are prized as having it to an abnormal degree. Throughout Indonesia, for example, the Dracoena terminalis is a plant, whose indomitable vitality the medicine-man tries to transfer to his patient. The sick are also rubbed with bezoar stones, and a hard candle-nut and a stone are placed both in the cradle of an infant and in the cradle of the ricebaby. The vitality in the hair shorn at a girl's first tonsure is considered so strong that it is buried at the foot of a barren tree to bring fruit as luxuriant as her tresses. In old days, Malay warriors, like Samson, wore their hair long and uncut. Saliva, too, is full of a man's vitality, so that there was a special courtier to guard a royal cuspidore. For everything connected with the body where vital force is present must be protected from the sorcery of enemies, as it was in Egypt and Babylon. A woman's blood can be employed to her hurt by a disappointed lover. Clippings from hair or nails are hidden or destroyed for fear possession of them may give an enemy control over their owner's vital force and endanger his life. This vital force exists even in one's shadow. There is a snail reputed to kill cattle by sucking their shadows. One should not walk upon a person's shadow, and the modern magician to vaunt his power will declare his shadow to be ‘the shadow of one beloved by Allah and the Prophet and angels forty and four’.

“We received a ceremonious visit about this time, from Pasqual's wife and daughter, and several other females, married and single, who, it appeared, were chosen a committee, to inform us that a lady of high rank, whose husband was absent on a visit to Huè, would do us the honour to come on board the ships on the following day, to gratify a desire she had long cherished to see the “Don-ong Olan,” and their ships; to this we returned a suitable answer, and at the time appointed the lady made her appearance, with several female attendants. She was, what would appear in one of our own fair countrywomen, to be about thirty-five, but in reality she was ten years younger, of a tall figure, rather embonpoint, and in appearance and manners, inclining to the masculine. Her visible garments, consisted of four robes of different colours; on her feet were Chinese slippers, and her head was encircled with a turban of yellow silk; one of her attendants carried her hat, another [331] her ornamented box, containing betel, &c. a third wielded an enormous fan, and a fourth a paper umbrella. Several golden bracelets encircled her wrists, and rings of the same metal, in which were precious stones of various colours, were on her fingers, which latter were outdone by the enormous nails growing from them. She attacked the entertainment we had provided for her, with considerable vigour, and tossed off several glasses of liquor with true bacchanalian grace. She passed the principal part of the afternoon on board the two vessels, enquiring the meaning and use of every novelty that met her view, and when towards evening she took leave, she thanked us very politely for our courtesy and attentions.”

"To carry out this procedure, the herder lassos the unmarked calf, draws it to him and to the ground, and marks the ears while sitting upon the left side of the animal, or another person may assist in holding the animal down. He cuts out the same pattern as borne by the cow which it was following. **One of the largest pieces of the ear pattern is not discarded with the rest, but placed in the mouth, then into the tunic pocket, to be later strung on a cord as a type of bookkeeping. These strings are seldom held separately by year or by individual owner in a family. Some persons cut a notch on the knife sheath or on a piece of wood, sometimes noting the calf's sex.** Corresponding notes of herd decrements are not made, though of course animals sold to the slaughterhouse are tallied there."

A searcher in Suonikylä disposes of four or five load reindeer, that will carry, among other things, forty straps, an ax, a gun, an extra pair of shoes, a lasso, hay for the shoes + = dried sedges that the Lapps use in their shoes in place of stockings. (Transl. note.) , a wind-shield, at least six loaves of bread, as well as cakes and salted fish. The excursion takes one and a half to two weeks in an area with a diameter of fifty to a hundred km. A wealthy reindeer owner may have several searchers at a time. **A searcher makes about three or four Fig. 383: “Counting stick”, on which the counted reindeer are marked. (in the lower drawing “spread out”): a) males, b) females, c) oxen, d) fawns, e) one-year olds.** Suonikylä. 1/3. excursions every autumn. Ten to twenty men meet at the “agreement-place” ( leht't-sajj [unknown] ). They may sometimes spend several days together, camping by a fire. Log fires ( [unknown]nuer't[unknown] s [unknown] ) are lit only when the cold is intense and shelters ( k[unknown] ovas ) are stretched only in rainy weather. They try to arrange agreement-places in different regions. When the reindeer have been “split”, the men return to their “autumn places”, close to which the herds are tended. During rut females are tethered. Near the autumn place reindeer are slaughtered for the herdsmen's use, those for sale only during the sleighing season. **When the reindeer are counted the owner may mark the number of his reindeer on a four sided stick (four faced) ( puaddz a -lohkkom-muorr ) with notches, which are marked with a knife on the edges of the stick; the males, oxen, females, fawns, and one year olds are marked on separate edges.** Formerly the females were not milked at all, except in Kolttaköngäs, but later this custom was acquired from the inhabitants of Inari. Autumn milking takes place at about nine a.m. and five p.m.; the milk is collected in reindeer rumens (first stomach). Late in fall, when there are no wolves, the herd is watched over as little as once a week, but when the beasts are threatening the herdsman is constantly present; dogs are not used very much in tending. The Kolts get together for Christmas, gathering the herds ( tsieyyâr ) in winter villages. 1 The description concerns the period before 1945. They tend the herds at twenty to forty km from the village, which is put up in a lichen-abounding region. Those with few reindeer gather in groups of two or three families, tending their animals together. The reindeer reserved for domestic use are kept tethered quite near the village, the house having also some lichen in store. Since the 1910's some western Kolts have left their herds at the autumn places, where they are tended in turn by family members. Occasionally people from Inari are hired as herdsmen ( t[unknown] sieyyarnik' ). In the winter village life is fairly free. Only during this century have they begun to practice freighting (e.g. for the Inari merchants). The “Kolt-reindeer” is superior to others, renowned for its size and bearing. A freight caravan may include even twenty draft reindeer; a journey between Inari village and Reisfiord yielded seven marks per sled in the 1910's."

p.714.

"Concerning reindeer there is a great abundance of beliefs, particularly among the reindeer-Lapps. The Lapps sometimes use indirect names for the reindeer and the herd, e.g. kâd'd[unknown] zâ = “hoof,' hil'bes-kâd'd[unknown] zâ = “proud hoof” = female reindeer, s[unknown] anâh = “fawn,” but this is not necessary. -- **A reindeer-Lapp never counts his animals, or they will end in the “number-limit,” i.e. reduce so much that they cannot be counted. Nor should he communicate to others the exact number of his reindeer, not even to the tax collectors**."

p.939

"**The verb lohkkâh (Finnish lukea = count, read) means counting (and reading). The number of reindeer was marked on a counting stick (K. puaddz a -rohkkom-muorr ), a 4-sided stick. In old times the Lapps, when taking goods on credit from the merchants who had to be paid at the same time the following year, used a counting stick (Lapp > Finnish kilkula ). The debt was marked on the stick, on which the Lapp made his own mark. A notch was cut on the stick for every rix-dollar, after which the stick was divided in two, one half being kept by the creditor, the other by the Lapp.** The counting-stick was also in use among the Finns, the Swedes and even many primitive peoples such as the Ostyaks. -- In addition to the word “a couple” (pair) (parrâ & Scandin.) the Lapps have another word meaning “two similar objects” = spârru (& Norwegian), K. sparr a “two dried codfish, hung up to dry from the tails; a double hook.” -- Kodtur , I. kodorv (probably & kodti [unknown] tóar'vi “a wild-reindeer-amount”) means all four flayed shank-skins ( k[unknown] amâs- kodtur ) of a slaughtered reindeer, or the tendons torn off all its legs, plus the back-tendons. -- The tendon-strings are twisted into rings of 20 pieces (K. p[unknown] arma h k' , I. suonn a -p[unknown] almag ). -- Bunches of dried sedges for shoes are twisted into a large ring ( suöi'dne-fierrâ ) of at least 150 pieces (I. reind.-L.). Rai'au is a caravan with 10 to 12 reindeer and a kóallus is a file of reindeer without vehicles, not more than 20. An eällu is a herd with more than 1,000 reindeer, a t[unknown] s[unknown] ora a herd with fewer than 1,000 reindeer, while a t[unknown] s[unknown] orrâyâ[unknown] s is a flock of a few hundred head (I. reind.-L.). These terms may also be considered as words indicating counting, although their use is restricted to a limited sphere."

Beach, H. (1981). Reindeer-herd management in transition: the case of Tuorpon Saameby in northern Sweden. In Acta Universitatis Upsaliensis. Uppsala studies in cultural anthropology (pp. xix, 542 , [17]  of plates (1 folded)). [Uppsala Universitet]; Distributed by Almqvist & Wiskell International. p.252.

"...**Anders G. Omma marks a calf by notching its ears with his unique, personal pattern. A reindeer's ear, marked in two different ways. The Saamish pattern of notches can be read on a running reindeer at considerable distance.** Lars Anders Blind delivers a calf to its rightful owner for marking. Besides the marking of calves, other husbandry chores, such as the castrating of bulls, may be performed in the summer; here, a young bull is being thrown to the ground. The herd separations at Parka begin around August 10. Nils Anders Blind pulls one of his reindeer to the Jokkmokk side of the corral, while Elli Karin, his sister, scares and prods the reindeer from behind. Alf Teilus, from Udtja forest Saameby, walks one over to the Jokkmokk side at Parka. A bull has been slaughtered for household consumption outside the Valli corral during the large, pre-rut, bull slaughter in September. Five dead buils at a time are transported by helicopter from the Valli mountain corral to the road's end in Kvikkjokk, where the slaughterhouse truck waits. December 1975. Nils Anders Blind leads the small sled caravan and covers the rear of the Viri Group's herd on its eastward migration to the lowlands. As the reindeer are gathered from the west, they are corralled in the lowlands for both separation and slaughter. The swirling herd surrounds itself with a cloud of snow mist. Around the perimeter of winter separation corrals, there are frequently numerous booths or “kontora”, into which herds can be broken down according to various, shifting, group constellations. The herder looks for his mark in a sea of reindeer. The exhausting work of herd separation is interrupted for coffee and a cigarette around a fire outside the corral. Separations are exciting events, which often the entire family attends. **Another winter chore is the reindeer count. Henrik Blind carries a paint brush on the end of a stick. A red paint spot signals that a reindeer has been counted and recorded under its owner's name. Henrik knows most of their earmarks by heart.** Ann-Katrin Blind asks her mother to check the reindeer-count list to see how many of her reindeer are present..."

## Southeastern Europe

### Greeks

Campbell, J. K. (1964). Honour, family and patronage: a study of institutions and moral values in a Greek mountain community. Clarendon Press. p.30.

"The Sarakatsan shepherd identifies himself with his animals. Their condition is almost as personal a concern as his own health and appearance. If a sheep is stoned by another man, the shepherd's honour is touched. In numbers and quality sheep are the prerequisite of prestige. He is aware of their dependence on him and of the dependence of his whole family on what the flock is able to supply. **He knows each animal, its history, and peculiarities. There is an extensive descriptive vocabulary of sheep terms. Skilled shepherds do not count their sheep, they scan them, recognizing at once the absence of an animal identified by a particular combination of markings, colours, and idiosyncrasies.** Sick sheep are tended with care and compassion. A shepherd may sleep with the animal under his cape to give it warmth. He is neither gentle nor sentimental towards his sheep but between the man and his animals there exists an evident solidarity."

# North America

## Eastern Woodlands

### Seminole

Garbarino, M. S. (1989). Economic development and the decision-making process on Big Cypress Indian Reservation, Florida. University Microfilms. p.73.

"However, included in the owner's share of 15 per cent there are still other possible charges: 1. Labor charges due; 2. House loans; 3. Water loans; 4. Short term loans; 5. Arts and crafts charges; 6. Others. It took a literate anthropologist a day to get this information. It was almost impossible for an illiterate Indian (who did not even know where to go for information) to get an explanation. Because Little Joe was behind in his loan payment (due to a very small calf crop) all his sales after operating costs and livestock commission had to be credited to repayment of interest and principal. This complicated accounting was very difficult for the old Indian to understand even when someone was willing to explain to him. Even after explanation it is doubtful whether he really grasped the reasons for his lack of cash income. The interviewer saw many cash sheets with the statement, “Net to Owner -0-.” Most of the recipients were as mystified as Little Joe. **Some of the Indians asked the interviewer to go to the agency and look up the size of loan still to be paid off, and sometimes even the size of the herd owned, particularly among old people who often cannot count beyond a dozen. They not only cannot keep track of their own herd size and calf crop, but have no grasp of the magnitude of the debt owed.** They do not understand percentages, and to go one step further, it may be assumed that they cannot conceive of the immense financial operation required to run a cattle industry. They understand only that their charges are so high that they absorb all the income from sales, and therefore, the promises of “money left over to spend for things” have not been fulfilled."

MacCauley, C. (1887). The Seminole Indians of Florida (pp. 469–531). Smithsonian Institution. p.525.

"As a guide towards a knowledge of the primitive manner of counting the method used by an old man in his intercourse with me will serve. He wished to count eight. He first placed the thumb of the right hand upon the little finger of the left, then the right forefinger upon the next left hand finger, then the thumb on the next finger, and the forefinger on the next, and then the thumb upon the thumb; leaving now the thumb of the right hand resting upon the thumb of the left, he counted the remaining numbers on the right hand, using for this purpose the fore and middle fingers of the left; **finally he shut the fourth and little fingers of the right hand down upon its palm, and raising his hands, thumbs touching, the counted fingers outspread, he showed me eight as the number of horses of which I had made inquiry**."

## Plains and Plateau


## Plains and Plateau

### Navajo

Roberts, J. M. (John M. (1951). Three Navaho households: a comparative study in small group culture. In Reports of the Ramah project; Papers: Vol. v. 40 (Issue 3, pp. xiii, 87 , plates). Published by the Museum. p.58-59.

"Someone in each household had kept tally by notching a stick. Elder Son B had kept count on the days he had worked for his Spanish-American employer by this method. **Grandfather C, Mother C, Father A, and Mother A specifically stated that they sometimes cut notches in sticks when counting sheep. Father A cut one notch for every hundred sheep; Mother A, one for every ten or fifteen sheep; Mother C, one for every ten sheep. It might be remarked that the herders did not have to count their sheep when they knew each sheep as an individual animal. Daughter B readily missed stray sheep from her flock, but she did not count them. As a matter of fact, she was not able to count very high.**

...

**Father B and Mother B said that they did not cut notches in sticks in tallying as did the others. Instead, they picked up rocks or sticks as an aid in counting. Father B said that he sometimes changed rocks from one hand to the other every twenty sheep.** Father B was the member most conversant with weights and measures because of his education and his experience working in a store. Grandfather B was the only person who could repeat the old Navaho names of months with certainty."

### Western Apache

Goodwin, G., & Goodwin, J. T. (1942). The social organization of the Western Apache. In Ethnological series (pp. xx, 701). The University of Chicago Press. p.381

"Property not left expressly under the control of a surviving mate or some other individual was ordinarily administered by the eldest or most influential living brother of the deceased, or, in the absence of brothers, by a maternal uncle or a sister's grown son. When the time came to distribute the property, the man in charge of it sent word to the widow or widower and the children and had the cattle rounded up. He gave so many head to each relative entitled to and desiring a share, at the same time setting aside a slightly greater portion for himself. The remainder, forming the largest part of the property, was turned over to the widow or widower and the deceased's children. **In dividing the property, it was common to apportion it by means of twigs or strips of yucca leaf, each standing for one animal.**"

## Melanesia

### Manus

Gustafsson, B. (1992). Houses and ancestors: continuities and discontinuities in in leadership among the Manus. IASSA. p.272.

"On occasions when exchanges of wealth between affinal kin were to be made, the men belonging to the same tali would gather in the men's house to prepare a meal consisting of meat. Usually they would cook the meat of a pig which had been received in the exchanges. The pig was taken to the men's house where it, after it had been killed, was covered with leaves and placed over a fire. Here it was left until all the bristle had disappeared. Then the meat was placed on banana leaves and cut into pieces. Each piece of meat was shared in groups of between two to four men. After receiving the meat, the men would take their piece, put it on fresh leaves and roast it between heated stones or over a wooden fire (Nevermann 1934: 190). The only part of the pig that was not distributed was the skull and maybe the intestines. The lower jaw bone was always saved. The bones, together with the jaw bones from pigs received in earlier affinal exchanges, were fastened onto one of the beams of the house. In the men's houses there would also be skulls from pigs, cuscus, and turtles. The skulls were often painted red, black, white and yellow, while geometrical patterns were carved onto the jaw bones (pp. 209–10). If there was a special young men's house in the village, the jaw bones from animals that had been prepared and eaten in this house would also be saved. **A man who had received a pig would always save the skull, or sticks symbolizing it, in order to be able to keep count of the number of distributions of wealth he had received** (p. 299)."

### Northeastern Massim

Damon, F. H. (1990). From Muyuw to the Trobriands: transformations along the northern side of the Kula Ring. University of Arizona Press. p.30.

"Counted things are not understood to make up a year, and years themselves are not counted. But the category “year” contains activities for which counting is important. Yams are planted once a year, people keep track of how many they plant, and, barring climatological crises, they anticipate how many they should be able to plant in a succeeding year. Mortuary rituals are conducted by any given actor at most once a year, and although there are many dimensions to these rituals, **the most important is the tally of pig debts existing before and after the ritual**. The only interisland sailing regime conceptually tied to times of the year, that between Budibud and Muyuw, runs according to strict quantitative dimensions. In Muyuw thought and experience, “quality” and “quantity” are complementary dimensions."

### Siwai

Oliver, D. L. (1955). A Solomon Island society: kinship and leadership among the Siuai of Bougainville. Harvard University Press. p.101.

"Potentially, then, it is possible for a Siuai to talk precisely in terms of, say, the 22nd house, 178 coconut palms, or 1000 leaves. **In actual usage, however, these natives seldom number most items past ten, the general qualifier “many” ( ponna ) is specific enough for most uses, except for such entities as pigs, sheets of thatch, shell money, and other items which are commonly utilized in large numbers.** Because of frequent use as a general standard of value, the set of numerical adjectives used to qualify spans of shell money occurs very frequently in utterances; and the set used to qualify certain hard and roundish items (shell-money discs, areca nuts, etc.) functions almost as an abstract numeration system because of the frequency of talk about large numbers of such items."

## Polynesia

### Tongans

Collocott, E. E. V. (Ernest E. V. (1927). Kava ceremonial in Tonga. The Journal of the Polynesian Society, Vol. 36, 21–47. p.26.

"Before any kava is prepared for drinking presentations of food and kava are brought and placed before the king and chiefs. These are arranged in orderly rows, pigs, yams, etc., and kava, so as to be easily viewed. Motu'apuaka directs that they be counted. **This is done by a man who walks along the rows of baskets, touching each in turn and counting in a loud voice. When he reaches ten a second man jumps up, holding a staff, and calls “one”; the first man continues counting to twenty, when the second man shouts “two,” and so on up to one hundred, when the second man calls “ten,” and a third man gets up, holding a staff, and shouts “one.” So they go on, the first man actually counting, the second keeping count of the tens, and the third of the hundreds. Should the number of baskets go into the thousands a fourth man would join in. When the counting is finished the result is formally announced, so many pigs** (distinguished by the way they are prepared and brought, which is some indication of size), so many plants, roots and bundles of kava (also distinguished by the way in which they are brought and size), so many baskets of yams, and perhaps other details are mentioned."

## Southern South America

### Abipón

Dobrizhoffer, M. (1822). An account of the Abipones, an equestrian people of Paraguay: volume 2. John Murray. p.168.

"Most of the American nations are extremely deficient in words to express number. The Abipones can only express three numbers in proper words. Iñtára, one. Iñoaka, two. Iñoaka yekainì, three. They make up for the other numbers by various arts: thus, Geyenk ñatè, the fingers of an emu, which as it has three in front and one turned back, are four, serves to express that number. Neènhalek, a beautiful skin spotted with five different colours, is used to signify the number five. If you interrogate an Abipon respecting the number of any thing, he will stick up his fingers, and say, leyer iri, so many. If it be of importance to convey an accurate idea of the number of the thing, he will display the fingers of both hands or feet, and if all these are not sufficient, show them over and over again till they equal the number required. Hence Hanámbegem, the fingers of one hand means five; Lanám rihegem, the fingers of both hands, ten; Lanám rihegem, cat gracherhaka anámichirihegèm, the fingers of both hands and both feet, twenty. **They have also another method of making up for want of numbers. When they return from an excursion to hunt wild horses, or shoot tame ones, none of the Abipones will ask them how many horses have you brought home? but, how much space will the troop of horse which you have brought home occupy? to which they will reply, the horses placed in a row would fill the whole market-place, or they extend from this grove to the river's bank. With this reply, which gives them an idea of the quantity of horses, they remain satisfied, though uninformed of the exact number. Sometimes they take up a handful of sand or grass, and showing it to the interrogator, endeavour in this way to express an immense quantity. But when number is spoken of, take care you do not readily credit whatever the Abipones say. They are not ignorant of arithmetic, but averse to it. Their memory generally fails them. They cannot endure the tedious process of counting.** Hence to rid themselves of questions on the subject, they show as many fingers as they like, sometimes deceived themselves, sometimes deceiving others. Often, if the number about which you ask exceed three, an Abipon, to save himself the trouble of showing his fingers, will cry Pòp! many. Chic leyekalipì, innumerable. Sometimes, when ten soldiers are coming, the assembled people will exclaim, Yoaliripì latenk naúertápek, a very great number of men are approaching."
